L2t: Ballot access laws that distinguish between established parties and other candidates have long been reviewed by courts under the Equal Protection Clause and the First Amendment.
L3t: States may require a reasonable showing of public support from independent and minor-party candidates, and courts uphold such requirements when the signature percentage and filing window are not unduly burdensome and the scheme treats party and non-party candidates comparably.
L4t: The court will likely uphold the statute as constitutional, since the 7% petition requirement and 180-day window serve legitimate state interests and do not violate equal protection.
L2f: The Supreme Court has held that all state restrictions on ballot access are subject to automatic invalidation because candidacy is a fundamental right.
L3f: Because the law gives established parties an easier route to the ballot than independents, it burdens independents' political expression and association so heavily that it cannot survive strict scrutiny under the free speech guarantees.
L4f: The court will most likely strike the statute down as unconstitutional because it violates the First and Fourteenth Amendment right of free speech.
